newsitem.title: FRANCE: Diplomatic calendar will challenge French rulers.
newsitem.headline: Diplomatic calendar will challenge French rulers.

text.p: New French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin plans to attend all forthcoming international summits, where he will accompany President Jacques Chirac, a source close to the premier said on Tuesday.
The move would be a serious attempt to limit the head of state's traditional pre-eminence in the conduct of foreign policy during a period of left-right power-sharing.

Major international events this month include a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17 and a summit of the Group of Seven rich nations in the U.S. city of Denver on June 20-22. NATO leaders are due to meet in Madrid on July 8-9.

"It is planned that Lionel Jospin will go to all these meetings," the source said. "It is quite normal that he should be with the president, all the more so because he has to get to know the representatives from other countries."
Jospin said during the campaign ahead of a Socialist-led parliamentary election victory on Sunday that France would speak with one voice on the international scene.
The two leaders have no known differences on the reform of European Union institutions, which is the major subject of the Amsterdam EU summit.

However, the Socialists are at odds with Chirac over France's approval of an EU "stability pact" to limit budget deficits after the launch of a single European currency, and have criticised the gradual reintegration of France into NATO.
Jospin is to make his first official trip abroad on Thursday, going to Malmo, Sweden, for a meeting of Socialist heads of government and parties, aides said.
He will address the meeting on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, who swept to power just one month ago.
The French constitution sets blurred dividing lines between the president's and the government's prerogatives on foreign and defence policy.
The president is responsible for signing treaties and upholding their enforcement, and is commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
But the prime minister "determines and conducts the policy of the nation" and is responsible for national defence.
Two previous periods of "cohabitation" between right-wing governments and the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand were largely harmonious on foreign policy after a bumpy start.

Chirac insisted on attending a G7 summit in Tokyo in 1986, a few weeks after he became prime minister in the first "cohabitation". The move caused protocol headaches for his Japanese hosts and Mitterrand humiliated Chirac by making him sit in the audience at the closing news conference.
Thereafter, Chirac left international summits to the president.
In 1993, new prime minister Edouard Balladur attended an EU summit in Copenhagen with Mitterrand's agreement, taking the seat normally reserved for the foreign minister.

He stood in for Mitterrand at some secondary international events when the head of state was ill with prostate cancer, but the president retained clear pre-eminence in foreign affairs and defence, barring the government from resuming nuclear testing.
